WHEN THE LABOUR GOVERNMENT SAYS IT CONSULTED THE PUBLIC, WHO DID IT CONSULT?

Earned Settlement · Home Office consultation findings

The Home Office’s own figures make for striking reading.

Only 18% identified as “British” citizens. The other 82% reported a different immigration or citizenship status. In fact, 73% were current visa holders.

Of the organisations that responded, 758 self-described as providing “immigration advice and/or support”. These included visa sponsoring organisations.

The Earned Settlement consultation survey was designed and hosted by the Home Office.

Most respondents disagreed with the proposed changes to the settlement framework (84% of individuals and 79% of organisations). Disagreement was higher among individuals with refugee status or humanitarian protection (89%) and current visa holders (86%) than among British Citizens.

Some of the most common themes in open text responses were the perceived unfairness of the proposed changes, particularly for those already on a path to settlement, and broad disagreement with extending baseline qualifying periods.

Views on criminal convictions: the majority of respondents were against a blanket ban on settlement for those with convictions.

The largest proportion of both individual and organisation respondents felt there should be no penalty for those applying for settlement who had claimed public funds.

Less than 50% agreed that giving back to the local community should be considered as a contribution to reduce the settlement qualifying period.

A larger proportion of open text responses said that those illegally entering the UK should not be penalised.

Organisations were largely negative about the impact of proposed changes. A majority anticipated that the changes would lead to additional administrative burden (73%) and would be detrimental to their ability to attract suitable candidates (71%), undertake workforce planning (71%), and retain existing migrant workers (70%). A majority also said the changes would make them less likely to sponsor visas in future (62%). Some said the changes would impact their plans to sponsor refugees and displaced people to work in the UK on a visa in the future (35%).

These are the figures behind Labour’s claim to have consulted the public on immigration policy.

This is the consultation Labour points to when defending its immigration policy. The public deserves to know who was actually involved in the consultation.

Source: Home Office, Earned Settlement: Public Consultation Findings
